Nodes.Title: Quickstart: a live shop in five calls

Nodes.Text:
This walks through the whole loop against the hosted sandbox deployment: create a shop with AI,
publish it, sell one unit through PayPal's sandbox, and ship it. Use `curl` as below, the **Try
It!** button on each endpoint page, or the SDKs (see **SDK Quickstart**).

**Base URL:** `https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com`. All payments are PayPal sandbox; no real
money moves. You need a PayPal sandbox **business** account email (the seller) and a
**personal** account (the buyer), from the
[PayPal developer dashboard](https://developer.paypal.com/dashboard/accounts). See
**Test in the PayPal sandbox** if you don't have them yet.
`createShop` takes a photo, a description or a link. A description alone is enough to start:

curl -X POST https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/shops \
  -F source=photo \
  -F "description=Hand-thrown stoneware mug, 12 oz, glazed in ocean blue. Dishwasher safe." \
  -F type=physical \
  -F price=34 \
  -F shipping=6 \
  -F stock=8 \
  -F ship_countries=US,CA \
  -F paypal_email=<your sandbox business email>

Add `-F photo=@mug.jpg` to send a photo; Gemini then reads the product from the picture too.
Gemini takes 15–40 seconds to design the page. The reply:

Keep `token`: it's the shop's **admin token**, it's shown only once, and every seller call needs
it in the `x-admin-token` header. `manageUrl` opens the same shop in the seller's web editor.

curl https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/shops/oceanmug \
  -H "x-admin-token: $TOKEN"

`spec` is the page design (headline, palette, layout, FAQ). `suggestions` lists sizes or colours
buyers may want to pick and questions they'll ask that the listing doesn't answer. To change the
design in words, call `refineShopDesign` with an instruction such as "make it feel more premium".

curl -X PATCH https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/shops/oceanmug \
  -H "x-admin-token: $TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "status": "live" }'

The shop is now open at `https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/oceanmug`. The same call changes
any setting you send (price, stock, link name), and the rest stay as they are.

Open the shop link in a browser and pay with the sandbox **personal** account, or choose
**Pay with Debit or Credit Card** and use a card from the sandbox credit card generator. You land
on the thank-you page.

Building your own checkout instead of using the shop page? Call `createCheckoutOrder` with the
`slug`, pass the PayPal order `id` it returns to the PayPal JavaScript SDK, and call
`captureCheckoutOrder` once the buyer approves.

curl https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/shops/oceanmug/orders \
  -H "x-admin-token: $TOKEN"

The paid order shows `fulfillment_status: to_ship` and the address PayPal collected. Mark it
shipped with its `id`:

curl -X POST https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/shops/oceanmug/orders/$ORDER_ID/ship \
  -H "x-admin-token: $TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "carrier": "USPS", "trackingNumber": "9400111899223817502345" }'
The tracking number is pushed to PayPal, so the buyer sees it in their PayPal activity.

- Sell an app or game instead of a physical item: **Sell an app or game with access codes**.
- Let AI shopping agents buy from the shop: **Let AI agents buy**.
- Get every paid and shipped order in Zapier: set `zapier_hook_url` (see **Webhooks**).
OneThing makes a one-product shop from a single input and takes payments with PayPal.

1. **Start.** Call `createShop` with a photo (`source=photo`), a link (`source=link`) or a
   product picked from `searchProducts` (`source=channel3`).
2. **AI draft.** Gemini works out what the product is, whether it's physical, digital or a
   recommendation, how it's delivered, the price, a short link and the page design. The
   response gives you the shop's `slug` and its admin `token`.
3. **Check and go live.** `getShop` shows the guesses. `updateShop` fixes anything that's off.
   Send `status: live` and the shop is open at `https://<host>/<slug>`.
4. **Get paid.** Buyers check out with PayPal. Physical orders arrive with the buyer's
   address; mark them shipped with `markOrderShipped` and PayPal shows the buyer the tracking.
   Digital orders get a private download link, or an access code (see the next guide).

Seller endpoints need the admin token in the `x-admin-token` header. Checkout, downloads and
access-code checks are public.

`signIn` takes an email address or a phone number: the first time creates the account, after that
it signs back in. Call `createShop` with the session cookie it sets and the shop belongs to that
account, so sellers find all their shops at `/account` without keeping each shop's private link.
On the website, sellers can also use **Log in with PayPal**, which records the PayPal account their
sales are paid into and fills it in on their shops.

A shop starts from one photo. `addPhotos` adds more (up to 8 in all) and `setPhotoOrder`
reorders or removes them; the first is the cover. With several photos, the shop page shows a
swipeable gallery, and buyers can open any photo full screen and page through the rest.

`connectPayPal` sends the seller through PayPal's onboarding, after which sales go straight to
their PayPal account; `getPayPalConnection` checks where that stands. A shop can also go live with
just a `paypal_email`.

Nodes.Title: Sizes, colours and the questions buyers will ask

Nodes.Text:
While drafting, Gemini also suggests what buyers will want to choose (sizes, colours with swatches)
and what they'll ask that the listing doesn't say, such as dimensions. They're saved as the shop's
`suggestions` and applied only when the seller confirms: `updateShop` with `options` (and stock per
combination in `option_stock`), and `facts` for the answers, which become product details.
`checkMissingDetails` asks again after an edit.

For colours, `matchColorPhotos` works out which photo shows each one and `setColorPhotos` saves
it, so the shop page switches photo when a buyer picks a colour. Checkout then takes the buyer's
pick as `options`, and the order records it.

Nodes.SuggestedLinkText: Sizes, colours and the questions buyers will ask

Nodes.Text:
A shop made from a store's product page, or from `searchProducts`, is a **recommendation**:
buyers purchase at the retailer through Channel3's tracked links, and the shop earns the
commission. These shops have `product_type: referral` and no PayPal checkout.

OneThing has two kinds of caller: the **seller**, who manages a shop, and everyone else
(buyers, the seller's own app, AI agents), who only use public endpoints.

`createShop` returns an admin token (32 random characters) once. Send it in a header on every
seller call:
x-admin-token: Xq3vT9kLm2…

The token belongs to one shop and never expires. Anyone who has it can change the shop, see its
orders and buyers' addresses, and take it offline, so keep it on a server, not in a web page.

A wrong or missing token answers **404**, the same as a shop that doesn't exist, so a token can't
be used to discover which shops exist.

Lost the token? A shop created while signed in also opens from the seller's `/account` page on
the website.

A marketplace that makes shops for its own sellers (a game store, a craft site) uses one
**platform API key** instead of keeping every shop's admin token:
Authorization: Bearer ot_sk_…

- **Making one:** sign in on the website with **Log in with PayPal** and open
  `/account/keys` (linked from `/account`). A typed email isn't enough: keys need a verified sign-in. The key is shown
  once; OneThing stores only a hash of it.
- **What it reaches:** shops created with it (and any other shop of the same account), through
  every seller endpoint. Another account's shop answers 404.
- **Return addresses:** the https origins you register on the key are the only places
  `connectPayPal` will send your sellers back to.
- **Revoking:** one click on `/account/keys`. Calls with it get 401 at once; the shops stay.
See **Build a marketplace on OneThing** for the whole flow.

`signIn` takes an email address or a phone number and sets an `ot_session` cookie (there's no
password or verification, since this deployment is sandbox only). Calling `createShop` with that
cookie makes the shop belong to the account, which lists all of the seller's shops at `/account`.
The cookie doesn't replace the admin token for the API: seller endpoints still need
`x-admin-token` or an API key.

On the website, sellers can also use **Log in with PayPal** (`logInWithPayPal`), which signs them
in and records the PayPal account their sales are paid into.
No auth at all:

| Endpoint | Used by |
|---|---|
| `checkLinkName`, `searchProducts` | The create-a-shop form |
| `getPayPalClientToken`, `createCheckoutOrder`, `captureCheckoutOrder` | The shop page's PayPal button |
| `verifyAccessCode` | The seller's own app or game |
| `downloadFile`, `getImage` | Buyers' browsers |
| `listAgentShops`, `getAgentProduct`, `getAgentOrder`, `openPayLink`, `callMcp` | AI shopping agents |

Checkout can't be abused to change a price: the amount always comes from the shop, never from
the request.

- `verifyAccessCode` accepts calls from any website, so a static web game can check codes
  straight from the browser.
- This docs portal's **Try It!** buttons are allowed too.
- Everything else is meant for servers and other non-browser clients. Seller calls in particular
  should come from your server, where the admin token stays private.
Every error is JSON with a sentence you can show to a person:
{ "error": "Photo must be an image under 8 MB.", "field": "photo" }

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `error` | What went wrong, written for the seller or buyer |
| `field` | The request field at fault, when there is one (handy for highlighting a form input) |
| `detail` | The upstream service's own message (Gemini, PayPal), for debugging only |

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | Something in the request needs fixing, or a step is missing (e.g. going live before uploading the file) | Show `error`; fix and resend |
| 404 | No such shop, or the admin token doesn't match it | Check the slug and `x-admin-token` |
| 409 | Taken or unavailable: a link name in use, a sold-out product or size. From `captureCheckoutOrder`: the buyer hasn't approved yet | Pick another; or keep polling capture |
| 410 | Gone: a download link that's used up or expired, or the last unit sold while the buyer was paying (they aren't charged) | Tell the buyer; nothing to retry |
| 422 | The buyer's card or PayPal funding was declined | Let them try another way to pay |
| 502 | Gemini, PayPal or Channel3 failed | Retry after a few seconds |
| 503 | That service isn't set up on this server | Not retryable |

Calls are safe to repeat where it matters: capturing an order that's already paid answers 200
again, and stock is only taken once per order.

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Photo sent to `createShop` | 8 MB |
| Each photo sent to `addPhotos` | 15 MB |
| Photos per shop | 8 |
| Digital file | 25 MB |
| Price | $0.50 – $10,000 (USD) |
| Shipping | $0 – $500 |
| Buyer options | 3 per shop (e.g. size, colour), 12 values each, 60 combinations |
| Download link | 5 downloads within 14 days |
| `refineShopDesign` instruction | 500 characters |
| `searchProducts` | 12 results |
| MCP `search_shops` | 25 results |

- `createShop` takes 15–40 seconds while Gemini designs the page. Hero art is made afterwards:
  poll `getShop` until `hero_status` is `ready` or `failed`.
- Gemini calls (`createShop`, `refineShopDesign`, `checkMissingDetails`, `matchColorPhotos`) can
  answer 502 when the model is busy. Wait a few seconds and send the same request again.

The hosted API at `https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com` runs entirely on PayPal's sandbox:
payments, payouts to sellers and seller onboarding all use test accounts, and no real money moves.
Real cards and real PayPal logins are refused.

1. Sign in to the [PayPal developer dashboard](https://developer.paypal.com/dashboard/accounts).
2. Under **Sandbox → Accounts**, PayPal has already made a **business** account and a
   **personal** account. Open each one to see its email and password.
   - **Business** is the seller: use its email as the shop's `paypal_email`, or connect it.
   - **Personal** is the buyer: log in with it at checkout.
3. To pay by card instead, open **Testing tools → Credit card generator** and use the card it
   makes on the **Pay with Debit or Credit Card** option.
A shop needs somewhere for the money to go before it can go live. Either:

- **Type an email:** `updateShop` with `paypal_email` set to the sandbox business email.
- **Connect PayPal:** `connectPayPal` returns a PayPal onboarding link. Open it, sign in with a
  sandbox business account and agree; PayPal sends you back to the shop's manage page.
  `getPayPalConnection` then reports `receivable` and `emailConfirmed`.

After a sale, the payment shows up in that sandbox business account at
[sandbox.paypal.com](https://www.sandbox.paypal.com).

| Try | How |
|---|---|
| Physical product | Pay, then `listOrders` shows the PayPal shipping address; `markOrderShipped` adds tracking |
| Digital file | `uploadDigitalFile` before going live; the thank-you page has the download link |
| Access code | `delivery: access_code` and `access_url`; check the code with `verifyAccessCode` |
| Sizes and colours | Set `options` with `updateShop`; pass the buyer's pick to `createCheckoutOrder` |
| Sold out | Set `stock: 1`, buy it, then try again: checkout answers 409 |
| AI agent | Call `create_order` on the MCP server, open `pay_url`, pay as the buyer, then `get_order` |

The API runs on `http://localhost:3000` (the **local** environment in the SDKs). One catch:
PayPal won't issue a client token for `localhost`, so the shop page doesn't show the PayPal
button there. Test checkout on the hosted deployment, or locally through the MCP server's
`create_order`, whose `pay_url` opens PayPal's own payment page.

The sandbox buyer has to be a PayPal account that doesn't receive the payment. PayPal refuses the
shop's own account, and for a shop without its own PayPal set up, the money goes to the platform
account, so that one is refused too. Use a **personal** sandbox account.

OneThing turns a photo, a link or a picked product into a live one-product shop that takes
PayPal payments, or a recommendation page that earns referral commissions through Channel3.
**How a shop is made**

1. `createShop`: start from a photo, a link, or a Channel3 product. Gemini guesses what it
   is, how it's delivered, the price, a short link and the page design. You get back the
   shop's link name and an **admin token**.
2. `updateShop`: correct anything the AI guessed, then set `status: live`.
3. Buyers pay on `https://<host>/<slug>` with PayPal. Sellers read orders and ship them.

**Auth.** Seller endpoints take the shop's admin token in the `x-admin-token` header, or a
**platform API key** (`Authorization: Bearer ot_sk_…`) for marketplaces that make shops for
their own sellers. Buyer endpoints (checkout, access-code verification, downloads) are public.

**Access codes.** A digital product can unlock an app or game instead of shipping a file.
Each paid order gets a code such as `K7QF-M2XP-9HTD`; your app calls `verifyAccessCode`
before unlocking. Raptor Rush on miriogames.com is a live example.

**Agent-ready.** Every live shop is also published for AI shopping agents: an MCP server at
`/api/mcp` with `search_shops`, `get_product`, `create_order` and `get_order`, and the same
four as plain GETs for assistants that can only fetch URLs (`listAgentShops`,
`getAgentProduct`, `orderByLink`, `getAgentOrder`), with `/llms.txt` as the starting point.
Order and status links also have short forms, `/<slug>/buy` and `/o/<order_id>/status`.
An agent can find and order, but the buyer still approves every payment at PayPal.

**Limits.** Calls that cost something are capped per network: 120 checkouts per 10 minutes,
10 new shops an hour and 60 AI requests an hour. Over the cap the reply is a 429 with
`Retry-After`.
All money moves through PayPal (sandbox in this deployment). OneThing never holds card data.

For additional package details, see the [Npm page for the one-thing-sdk@1.0.0 npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/one-thing-sdk/v/1.0.0).

OneThing's API is built for **platforms with many sellers**: a game portal, a craft site, a
course library. The platform keeps its own catalog and pages; OneThing makes each seller a shop
and runs the PayPal checkout, and **every sale is paid straight to that seller's own PayPal
account**. The platform never holds anyone's money.

**Worked example:** the [Mirio Games marketplace](https://www.miriogames.com/market/) lets indie
developers upload an HTML game and sell it. It's static pages on S3 plus one serverless function
that calls OneThing through the TypeScript SDK generated from this portal.

On the website, **Log in with PayPal**, open `/account/keys` (linked from `/account`), and make a key with
your site's origin as a return address (`https://www.miriogames.com`). Keep it in your server's
secrets; never put it in a web page.

Nodes.Title: 2. Make a shop for a seller

Nodes.Text:
When a seller lists something, create a shop with your key. It belongs to your account, so the
key manages it from now on:

Nodes.SuggestedLinkText: 2. Make a shop for a seller

Nodes.Text:
PayPal walks the seller through signing in (or opening a business account) and sends them back to
your `returnUrl` with `?paypal=connected&shop=<slug>`. `getPayPalConnection` confirms it.

Buyers pay on the shop page (`result.shops[i].url`). Going live is refused until the seller's
PayPal account can be paid, so no sale is ever made to nowhere.

With `delivery: access_code`, the buyer's thank-you page links to your `access_url` with
`?code=…`. Check it before unlocking:

Mirio Games goes one step further: game files sit in a private S3 prefix, and only a valid code
gets a 60-second download link, so the game can't be fetched without buying it.

Nodes.Title: What the platform gets for free

Nodes.Text:
- Sellers' orders, shipping and refunds through PayPal; `listOrders` for your dashboards.
- Every shop is also on OneThing's MCP server, so AI shopping agents can find and buy your
  sellers' products (see **Let AI agents buy**).

Nodes.SuggestedLinkText: What the platform gets for free

Nodes.Title: Sell an app or game with access codes

Nodes.Text:
A digital product doesn't have to be a file. Set `delivery: access_code` and `access_url` to
where your app runs; every paid order then gets a unique code like `K7QF-M2XP-9HTD`.

After paying, the buyer lands on the thank-you page with the code and a **Start now** button
that opens `access_url?code=<code>`.
Your app checks the code before unlocking:
{ "valid": true, "product": "Raptor Rush: Browser Edition" }

The endpoint is open to any origin, so a static web game can call it straight from the
browser. It accepts the shop's current and former link names, and codes typed in lower case
or without dashes. Each check is counted (`code_uses` on the order).

**Live example:** [Raptor Rush](https://www.miriogames.com/raptor-rush/play/) on miriogames.com
is sold at [/raptorrush](https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/raptorrush) and unlocks with
this call.

Nodes.SuggestedLinkText: Sell an app or game with access codes

Nodes.Text:
Every live shop is agent-ready. An AI shopping agent can find it, read the product and place an
order, and the buyer approves the payment at PayPal. No agent can spend someone's money on its own.
There are two ways in, depending on what the agent can do:

| The agent can… | Use | Find | Read | Order | Check the order |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Call MCP tools (Claude, ChatGPT Developer Mode, Grok, agent SDKs) | The MCP server | `search_shops` | `get_product` | `create_order` | `get_order` |
| Only fetch URLs (free-tier ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini; plain HTTP) | Plain GETs | `listAgentShops` | `getAgentProduct` | `orderByLink` | `getAgentOrder` |

Both return the same JSON. Every live shop page also carries its facts as schema.org `Product`
JSON-LD and links to its product JSON (`<link rel="alternate" type="application/json">`), so
agents that browse find them too.

An AI assistant without MCP (free-tier ChatGPT or Gemini, for example) won't find the API on its
own. Give it one URL:
> Read https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/llms.txt and help me buy something from the gallery.
curl https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/llms.txt

It's plain text, written for models: the gallery's shops with their prices, product JSON links
and order links, then how to buy in three steps (open the order link, show the buyer `pay_url`,
open `status_url` once they've paid) and how to search, read and check orders. Every page on the site links to it, and the home page
and gallery show the link as text too.

Buyers have the best experience with short replies and clickable links. Every product, order
and order-status reply (JSON and MCP alike) includes `show_buyer`: a suggested reply in Markdown
with the links already written as links. Showing it as written, with little else, is
recommended but never required. Along the way the buyer sees:

1. The product, its price and the choices: `Size: 7 · 8 · 9`, then `Which size?`
2. Once they've picked and said to buy: `**[Pay $255.00 with PayPal](…)**`
3. Once paid: what they got (access code, download link or shipping details) and `[Your receipt](…)`

Every reply also carries `agent_name`: who the request was credited to in the seller's stats, so
you can confirm the name you gave was received.
No key, no session. These samples use the hosted sandbox deployment.

**Say who you are (optional).** Add `agent=<your name>` to a product or order link
(`?agent=my-shopping-bot`, or `&agent=…` after option picks) and the seller's stats show your
agent by name. A recognised user agent (`ChatGPT-User`, `Claude-User`…) takes precedence. The
reply's `agent_name` says who was credited, and the order and status links it returns carry your
name on, so you only add it once.
curl "https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/agent/shops?q=skates&limit=5"

Leave out `q` to list the newest gallery shops. Shops matching more of the words come first, and
browsing words ("something interesting to buy") are ignored. A query that matches nothing gets
the newest shops instead, with `"matched": false` and a `show_buyer` that says so, rather than an
empty list. Only shops approved for the gallery are listed; any live shop can still be read by its
link name.
curl https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/agent/shops/vintageskates

{
  "shop": "vintageskates",
  "name": "Vintage Cream and Red Roller Skates",
  "kind": "physical",
  "price": { "amount": 240, "currency": "USD", "label": "$240.00" },
  "shipping": { "amount": 15, "currency": "USD", "ships_to": ["US"] },
  "total": { "amount": 255, "currency": "USD" },
  "delivery": "Shipped. PayPal collects the buyer's address at checkout.",
  "availability": "in_stock (9 left)",
  "how_to_buy": "Call create_order on the OneThing MCP server, then give the buyer its pay_url to pay at PayPal.",
  "mcp_server": "https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/mcp"
}

(Shortened: the full reply also has the description, highlights, details, FAQ, images and, when
the buyer picks a size or colour, `options` and `variants` with stock for each.)
`total` already includes shipping, so an agent can quote the real price.

An assistant that can only fetch URLs can't send the POST that `create_order` is, so each product
also has an order link: a GET that places the order. The product JSON spells it out
(`order_url`, or `variants[].order_url` per size or colour), and so does `/llms.txt`, because
some assistants only open URLs they've been shown.
curl "https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/vintageskates/buy?Size=9"

{
  "order_id": "pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe",
  "status": "awaiting_buyer_approval",
  "total": "$255.00",
  "options": { "Size": "9" },
  "pay_url": "https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/o/pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe",
  "status_url": "https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/o/pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe/status",
  "next_step": "Show pay_url to the buyer as a link. …"
}

Nothing is charged: the assistant shows the buyer `pay_url`, and they pay at PayPal. Every
request makes a new order, so open the link once, after the buyer says to buy. Option names and
values aren't case-sensitive; a missing or unknown one gets a 400 that lists the valid values.

The order link is `/<shop>/buy`, short so a buyer can read it; `/api/agent/shops/<shop>/order`
is the same endpoint. Known crawlers and link previewers get a 403 (they're also kept out by
`robots.txt`), and one network can place 120 orders per 10 minutes before getting a 429 with
`Retry-After`.
curl https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/o/pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe/status

{
  "order_id": "pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe",
  "status": "paid",
  "product": "Raptor Rush: Browser Edition",
  "amount": { "item": 2.99, "shipping": 0, "total": 2.99, "currency": "USD" },
  "total": "$2.99",
  "paid_at": "2026-10-22T03:12:50Z",
  "receipt_url": "https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/raptorrush/thanks?order=pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe",
  "delivery": {
    "type": "access_code",
    "access_code": "K7QF-M2XP-9HTD",
    "start_url": "https://www.miriogames.com/raptor-rush/play/?code=K7QF-M2XP-9HTD"
  }
}

This is the `status_url` an order link or `create_order` returns (`/api/agent/orders/<id>` is the
same endpoint). An order the buyer placed on the shop page can be checked too, from the
`?order=` in their thank-you page link.

Nodes.Title: When a person clicks the link

Nodes.Text:
Assistants sometimes hand the buyer a link instead of opening it. A person clicking one in a
browser gets a page, not JSON: the product link goes to the shop page (add `?view=json` to read
the JSON), the order link goes straight to PayPal (or to the shop page if a size or colour is
missing), and the status link goes to the receipt. A "person" is a browser navigation the user
started (`Sec-Fetch-User: ?1`); known assistants and headless browsers always get JSON.

Nodes.Text:
Add `https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/mcp` to any MCP client as a Streamable HTTP server,
with no authentication. For Claude Code:
claude mcp add --transport http onething https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/mcp

The server is stateless: each POST carries one JSON-RPC 2.0 message and gets a plain JSON reply.
The one exception is the `Mcp-Session-Id` header on the `initialize` reply: it carries your
`clientInfo.name`, and sending it back on later requests is how the seller's stats show which
agent sent the buyer. MCP clients do all of this for you; the raw requests below are for testing and for building
your own client.

curl -X POST https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/mcp \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":0,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"my-agent","version":"1.0"}}}'

curl -X POST https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/mcp \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -H "mcp-session-id: <the Mcp-Session-Id from initialize>" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
There are four tools:

1. `search_shops` finds live gallery shops by keywords (`query`, `limit`).
2. `get_product` describes one (`shop`), including any `options` the buyer must pick.
3. `create_order` puts one unit on order (`shop`, `options`) and returns `pay_url`. Nothing is charged yet.
4. `get_order` (`order_id`) reports where the order stands, and once it's paid, what the buyer got.

Hosts that draw MCP Apps UI, such as ChatGPT, also get a product card: `resources/read` on
`ui://onething/shop-card-v1.html` returns it, and the tools point to it. The card shows the real photos,
options and a Pay with PayPal button, so for those hosts `show_buyer` is a one-line note instead of
Markdown. Each tool says whether it only reads (`annotations.readOnlyHint`); only `create_order`
changes anything.

curl -X POST https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/mcp \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"search_shops","arguments":{"query":"skates"}}}'

curl -X POST https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/mcp \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_product","arguments":{"shop":"vintageskates"}}}'

Every tool reply has the answer twice: as JSON text in `content` (for models) and as an object
in `structuredContent` (for code). The objects are the same as the plain GETs above.

curl -X POST https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/mcp \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"create_order","arguments":{"shop":"vintageskates","options":{"Size":"9"}}}}'
`structuredContent`:

{
  "order_id": "pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe",
  "status": "awaiting_buyer_approval",
  "total": "$255.00",
  "options": { "Size": "9" },
  "pay_url": "https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/o/pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe",
  "status_url": "https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/o/pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe/status",
  "next_step": "Show pay_url to the buyer as a link. It opens PayPal, where they pay (and enter a shipping address for physical items). When they say they've paid, call get_order with order_id: it returns the access code, download link or shipping details."
}

The price comes from the shop, never from the agent. Leave out `options` for a product without
them; a missing or sold-out pick comes back as a tool error (`isError: true`) the model can read.

`pay_url` is a link on OneThing (`/o/<order_id>`, see `openPayLink`) that redirects to PayPal.
PayPal's own approval URL carries a checkout token, and agent platforms hide tokens like that from
chat as secrets, so an agent could never show it. `pay_url` is safe to print: the token stays on
the server. Once the order is paid, the same link opens the thank-you page instead.
curl -i https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/o/pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe

HTTP/1.1 303 See Other
location: https://www.sandbox.paypal.com/checkoutnow?token=…

An agent in a chat can't sit and poll. The rhythm that works: show `pay_url` as a link, wait for
the buyer to say they've paid, then call `get_order` once.

curl -X POST https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/api/mcp \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_order","arguments":{"order_id":"pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe"}}}'
A paid physical order's `structuredContent`:

{
  "order_id": "pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe",
  "status": "paid",
  "product": "Vintage Cream and Red Roller Skates",
  "options": { "Size": "9" },
  "amount": { "item": 240, "shipping": 15, "total": 255, "currency": "USD" },
  "total": "$255.00",
  "paid_at": "2026-10-22T02:41:37Z",
  "receipt_url": "https://one-thing-ash0.onrender.com/vintageskates/thanks?order=pX4kR9tVb2nQ7sLe",
  "delivery": {
    "type": "shipping",
    "ship_to": { "name": "Sam Rivera", "address": "1 Main St, Springfield, IL, 62701, US" },
    "fulfillment": "to_ship",
    "tracking": null
  }
}
`delivery` is one of:

| `type` | Fields |
|---|---|
| `access_code` | `access_code`, and `start_url` (the seller's app with the code filled in) |
| `download` | `download_url` (works 5 times over 14 days) |
| `shipping` | `ship_to`, `fulfillment` (`to_ship` or `shipped`), `tracking` once shipped |
When a payment doesn't go through, `status` says why and `next_step` says what to do:

| `status` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `awaiting_buyer_approval` | Not paid yet. `pay_url` is included again. |
| `declined` | PayPal declined it; nothing charged. The buyer can open `pay_url` again. |
| `sold_out` | It sold out before the payment was captured; nothing charged. |
| `expired` | The PayPal checkout expired; call `create_order` for a new one. |
| `failed` | PayPal couldn't be reached; call `get_order` again. |
The seller sees these orders in `listOrders` with `channel: agent`.

Pay with a **personal** sandbox account that doesn't receive the money. PayPal refuses the shop's
own account, and for a shop without its own PayPal set up, the money goes to the platform account,
so that one is refused too. See **Test in the PayPal sandbox**.

Nodes.Title: Create Shop
Nodes.Name: createShop
Nodes.Description:
Starts a draft shop from one of three sources. Gemini designs the page and guesses the
setup; check it with `getShop`, adjust with `updateShop`, then go live.

Sent with a session cookie from `signIn`, the shop belongs to that account, which also
becomes its seller email (and PayPal email, after Log in with PayPal) unless you give one.

- `source=photo`: a `photo` and/or a `description` of your own product.
- `source=link`: a `url`. If Channel3 recognises it as a store's product page, the shop
  becomes a recommendation (`product_type: referral`); otherwise the page is read and you
  sell the product yourself with PayPal.
- `source=channel3`: a `productId` from `searchProducts` (a recommendation).

Takes 15–40 seconds. Hero art, if available, is generated afterwards (`hero_status`).

**Platforms:** sent with a platform API key, the shop belongs to the key's account, so the
key can manage it from then on (no need to keep the admin token). It's made for one of the
platform's sellers, so it inherits nothing from the account: set `paypal_email` or call
`connectPayPal` for that seller.

Nodes.Title: Connect Pay Pal

Nodes.Description:

returned `url`; they sign in to PayPal (or create a business account) and grant OneThing
permission. PayPal brings them back to `/api/shops/<slug>/paypal/return`, which saves the
connection and opens the manage page. From then on, sales are paid to that account.

page instead, as `returnUrl?paypal=connected|incomplete|cancelled|failed&shop=<slug>`. The
URL's origin must be one registered on the key.

Nodes.Title: Order by Link
Nodes.Name: orderByLink
Nodes.Description:
Orders one unit with a GET: the MCP `create_order` tool for AI assistants that can only
fetch URLs, such as free-tier ChatGPT or Grok. Nothing is charged. The reply has `pay_url`,
where the buyer pays at PayPal, and `status_url` (`getAgentOrder`), which says when they
have and what they got.

For a product with options, pass the buyer's pick as query parameters named after the
options (`?Size=9`, or `?Color=Ice+Blue&Size=L`); names and values are matched without
regard to case. You rarely build this URL yourself: `getAgentProduct` and `/llms.txt`
write it out in full (`order_url`, or `variants[].order_url`), because some assistants
only open URLs they have been shown.

Every request makes a new order, so open it once, after the buyer says to buy. Known
crawlers and link previewers get a 403 (and are kept out by `robots.txt`); any other
leaves an unpaid order at most, since stock is only taken when a payment is captured.
Replies are `no-store` and `X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow`.

`/<slug>/buy` is the same endpoint at a short URL, and the one `order_url` uses.
A person clicking the link in a browser (`Sec-Fetch-User: ?1`) is redirected instead; known assistants and headless browsers always get JSON. It goes straight to `pay_url`, or to the shop page when an option is missing
or unknown.

Nodes.Title: Call Mcp
Nodes.Name: callMcp
Nodes.Description:
A [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server, so agents such as
Claude can shop here. Add `https://<host>/api/mcp` to an MCP client as a Streamable HTTP
server. It's stateless: each POST carries one JSON-RPC 2.0 message (or a batch) and gets a
plain JSON reply, with no event stream. The `initialize` reply's `Mcp-Session-Id` header
carries the client's `clientInfo.name`; send it back on later requests (MCP clients do)
so the seller's stats show which agent sent the buyer. Nothing else is kept.

Methods: `initialize`, `ping`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, and `resources/list`,
`resources/templates/list` and `resources/read` for the product card. Each tool carries
`annotations` (only `create_order` isn't `readOnlyHint`). Tools:

| Tool | Arguments | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `search_shops` | `query?`, `limit?` (1–25) | Live gallery shops, best match first; no match returns the newest with `matched: false` |
| `get_product` | `shop` | The same object as `getAgentProduct` |
| `create_order` | `shop`, `options?` | One unit on order; returns `order_id` and `pay_url` |
| `get_order` | `order_id` | Status and `next_step`; once paid, the receipt and `delivery` |

**The buyer always approves.** `create_order` charges nothing: the agent shows the buyer
`pay_url` (`/o/<order_id>`, see `openPayLink`), which opens PayPal. It's a plain link on this
site, so agent platforms that hide PayPal's checkout tokens can still show it. When the buyer
says they've paid, the agent calls `get_order`.

`get_order` status is one of `awaiting_buyer_approval`, `paid`, `declined` (nothing charged;
the buyer can open `pay_url` again), `sold_out`, `expired` (call `create_order` again) or
`failed` (PayPal couldn't be reached; try again), with a `next_step` the agent can follow.
A paid order carries `delivery`: `{type: access_code, access_code, start_url?}`,
`{type: download, download_url}` or `{type: shipping, ship_to, fulfillment, tracking}`, plus
`amount` with item, shipping and total. Orders made this way show `channel: agent` in
`listOrders`.

**The product card.** Hosts that draw MCP Apps UI (ChatGPT, or a client that declares the
`io.modelcontextprotocol/ui` extension) get `search_shops`, `get_product` and
`create_order` results as a card with the real photos, options and a Pay with PayPal button
(`ui://onething/shop-card-v1.html`). For them `show_buyer` is a one-line note rather than
Markdown, so the model doesn't repeat or invent what the card shows.

Tool errors (an unknown shop, a sold-out size, over the checkout cap) come back as results
with `isError: true`, so the model can read them and try something else.

Nodes.Text: The SDK client can be initialized directly from a JSON configuration file using the `fromJsonConfig` static method available on the `Client` class.` This allows you to store and load configuration settings from JSON files, making it easier to organize and manage different configurations across environments.
Node.js Environment
In Node.js environments, you can use the `fs` module to read the configuration file from the file system.
Browser Environment
In browser environments, you can use the `import` function to load the configuration file.
Example Configuration File

The SDK client can be initialized directly from environment variables using the `fromEnvironment` static method available on the `Client` class. This allows you to configure the SDK through environment variables, making it easier to manage different settings across different environments.
Node.js Environment
In Node.js environments, you can use the `dotenv` package to load environment variables from a `.env` file and pass `process.env` to the configuration.
The `fromEnvironment` method accepts an optional parameter for environment variables. If not provided, it defaults to `process.env`.
Browser Environment

In browser environments, you can pass configuration values directly as key-value pairs to the `fromEnvironment` method.  Since `process.env` is not available in browsers, environment variables must be passed as an object.
Example .env File

# Basic Configuration
TIMEOUT=30000
ENVIRONMENT=production

# Authentication Credentials
ADMIN_TOKEN_X_ADMIN_TOKEN=x-admin-token
PLATFORM_KEY_ACCESS_TOKEN=accesstoken

# Retry Configuration
MAX_NUMBER_OF_RETRIES=3
RETRY_ON_TIMEOUT=true
RETRY_INTERVAL=10
MAX_RETRY_WAIT_TIME=120
RETRY_BACKOFF_FACTOR=2
HTTP_STATUS_CODES_TO_RETRY=408,413,429,500,502
HTTP_METHODS_TO_RETRY=GET,PUT,DELETE

# Proxy Settings
PROXY_ADDRESS=http://localhost:3000
PROXY_PORT=8080
PROXY_AUTH_USERNAME=username
PROXY_AUTH_PASSWORD=password
